content: Alternaria alternata is a fungal species that has been documented to infect over 380 different host species. It acts as an opportunistic pathogen, causing a variety of plant diseases such as leaf spots, rots, and blights, which can affect multiple parts of the plant. In humans, it is known to cause upper respiratory tract infections in individuals with AIDS and can trigger asthma in people who are sensitive to it. The conidiophores of Alternaria alternata are either straight or slightly curved and arise directly from the substrate. These structures form bushy heads composed of 4 to 8 large, catenate (chain-like) conidia. Secondary conidiophores are typically short and consist of a single cell. The conidia of this fungus are pale brown to light brown in color. They exhibit a range of shapes, including obclavate (inversely club-shaped), obpyriform (inversely pear-shaped), or ellipsoid. Some conidia have a short conical beak at the tip, while others are beakless. The surface of the conidia can vary from smooth to verruculose (finely warted). The size of the conidia ranges from 20–63 µm in length and 9–18 µm in width, with mature conidia typically measuring 10–30 µm by 5–12 µm when grown on potato carrot agar (PCA). The conidia are septate, containing several vertical and up to 8 transverse septa. On PCA, they typically exhibit 3–7 transverse septa and 1–5 longitudinal septa. The fungus produces chains of conidia that are often branched and can form long chains with more than 5 conidia. On PCA, individual chains may consist of 5–15 conidia, and complex branching chains can contain as many as 50–60 conidia.
